The [Scientific Calculator](/scientific-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Free online scientific calculator with trigonometry, logarithms, powers, factorials and unit conversions. Open it and start straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like. It is one of the [Math tools](/tools?category=Math) on CalcHub — the others work the same way.

This free online scientific calculator handles everything a classroom or engineering calculator does: sine, cosine and tangent with their inverses, hyperbolic functions, natural and common logarithms, powers and roots, factorials, π and e, plus a built-in unit converter for length, mass, area, volume, angle, speed, energy, pressure and temperature. Type an expression with your keyboard or tap the keys — the result previews live as you type, and the last eight answers stay in your history. Everything runs in your browser, so nothing you enter leaves your device.

## How to use the Scientific Calculator

Open the [Scientific Calculator](/scientific-calculator) and start straight away — there is no form to fill in first. The result updates as you work, so you can try different settings and see the change straight away.

1. Choose DEG or RAD to set how angles are interpreted for sin, cos and tan.
2. Type an expression such as 3*sin(45)^2 or tap the on-screen keys. A live preview shows the answer as you go.
3. Press = or Enter to calculate. The result is stored as Ans for your next calculation.
4. Click any line in History to reload that expression and edit it.
5. Scroll to Unit conversions, pick a quantity, enter a value and choose the from/to units. Use the swap button to reverse the conversion.

## Formula

Expressions follow standard order of operations (PEMDAS/BODMAS): parentheses, then functions and factorials, then exponents (right to left, so 2^3^2 = 2^9), then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. Trigonometric functions use the selected angle mode: in DEG mode sin(x) = sin(x × π/180). log is base 10, ln is base e (≈ 2.71828).

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Scientific Calculator](/scientific-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. In DEG mode, sin(30) + log(1000) = 0.5 + 3 = 3.5. In RAD mode, cos(pi) = −1. 5! = 120, sqrt(144) = 12 and 2^10 = 1024. In the converter, 1 mile = 1.609344 km and 100 °C = 212 °F. Try the same figures in the [Scientific Calculator](/scientific-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## Trying it out

The fastest way to see what the [Scientific Calculator](/scientific-calculator) does is to open it and enter values you already know the answer for. Change one input at a time and watch how the result responds — that tells you more than any description. Everything runs in your browser, so you can experiment freely: nothing is saved, sent or tracked.

## Trigonometric functions

sin, cos and tan take an angle and return a ratio; sin⁻¹ (asin), cos⁻¹ (acos) and tan⁻¹ (atan) do the reverse and return an angle in the current mode. Common values: sin(30°) = 0.5, cos(60°) = 0.5, tan(45°) = 1. tan(90°) is undefined and returns an error. Hyperbolic functions sinh, cosh and tanh can be typed directly.

## Degrees vs radians

A full circle is 360 degrees or 2π radians, so 1 rad ≈ 57.2958°. School geometry usually uses degrees; calculus, physics and programming usually use radians. If an answer looks wrong — for example sin(90) giving 0.894 — you are probably in RAD mode.

## Logarithms and exponents

log(x) is the common logarithm (base 10), so log(1000) = 3. ln(x) is the natural logarithm (base e), so ln(e) = 1. log2(x) gives base-2 logs. To use any other base b, apply the change-of-base rule: log_b(x) = ln(x) / ln(b). exp(x) equals e^x, and x^y raises any number to a power, including fractions such as 27^(1/3) = 3.

## Roots, factorials and percentages

sqrt(x) returns the square root and cbrt(x) the cube root. n! multiplies every whole number from 1 to n (valid for 0 to 170). The % sign divides by 100, so 200*15% = 30. abs(x) returns the absolute value.

## Implicit multiplication and constants

You can write 2pi, 3(4+1) or 2sin(30) without a × sign. π ≈ 3.14159265 and e ≈ 2.71828183 are built in, and Ans recalls your previous result. Very large or very small results are shown in scientific notation, e.g. 6.02e23.

## Supported unit conversions

Length (mm, cm, m, km, in, ft, yd, mi), mass (mg, g, kg, t, oz, lb), area (cm², m², km², ft², acre, ha), volume (mL, L, m³, US gallon, US cup, fl oz), angle (deg, rad, grad, arcmin, arcsec), speed (m/s, km/h, mph, knot), energy (J, kJ, cal, kcal, Wh, kWh), pressure (Pa, kPa, bar, atm, psi) and temperature (°C, °F, K). All factors use exact international definitions where they exist.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Use parentheses generously: -3^2 = −9, but (-3)^2 = 9.
- Check the DEG/RAD toggle before any trigonometry question.
- Press Enter on your keyboard instead of clicking =.
- Use Ans to chain multi-step calculations without retyping.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is this scientific calculator free?

Yes. It is completely free, needs no sign-up and works on phones, tablets and computers. There is no limit on how often you use it, nothing to install, and no account to create — open the [Scientific Calculator](/scientific-calculator) and start straight away.

### How do I switch between degrees and radians?

Use the DEG / RAD toggle above the display. It affects sin, cos, tan and their inverses. Try it with your own numbers in the [Scientific Calculator](/scientific-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is the difference between log and ln?

log is the base-10 logarithm and ln is the natural logarithm with base e ≈ 2.71828. For example log(100) = 2 and ln(e²) = 2. Try it with your own numbers in the [Scientific Calculator](/scientific-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### How do I calculate a log with a different base?

Use the change-of-base formula: log_b(x) = ln(x) / ln(b). For log base 3 of 81, enter ln(81)/ln(3) = 4. Try it with your own numbers in the [Scientific Calculator](/scientific-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Why does tan(90) show an error?

Tangent of 90° is undefined because cos(90°) = 0, so the calculator reports it instead of returning a misleading huge number. Try it with your own numbers in the [Scientific Calculator](/scientific-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
